summary.text: A self-avoiding walk is a sequence of moves on a lattice that never visits the same point more than once.
It models chain-like molecules such as polymers and proteins, whose physical volume keeps two parts of the chain from sitting in the same spot.
Very little is known rigorously about it, and its properties cannot be calculated analytically, so researchers rely on numerical simulations.

paragraphs.heading: A walk that never repeats
paragraphs.text: A self-avoiding walk, or SAW, is a string of moves on a lattice that never lands on the same point twice. In graph theory terms, it is a special kind of path. If such a walk closes up into a loop, it is called a self-avoiding polygon, or SAP. In computational physics, a SAW is pictured as a chain of nodes in two or three dimensions, usually with steps of fixed length, that never crosses itself or any other walk.

paragraphs.heading: Why chemists care
paragraphs.text: The chemist Paul Flory may have been the first to use SAWs. He wanted to model chain-like things such as polymers and solvents, whose bulk stops two pieces from filling the same spot in space. A group of SAWs obeys what is called the excluded volume condition. SAWs and SAPs are now central to modelling how thread-like and loop-like molecules, such as proteins, tangle and knot.

paragraphs.heading: Hard to pin down
paragraphs.text: Mathematicians have proved very little about the self-avoiding walk. Physicists have offered many conjectures that are believed true and are backed strongly by computer simulations. Its properties cannot be worked out analytically, so simulations do the heavy lifting. Even counting how many walks exist on a given lattice has no known formula, only rigorous ways to approximate the answer.

paragraphs.heading: The pivot algorithm
paragraphs.text: A common way to simulate these walks is the pivot algorithm, a Markov chain Monte Carlo method. It takes an existing walk and picks a random point on it. Then it rotates or reflects the part of the walk that comes after that point, producing a new walk.

paragraphs.heading: How big a walk gets
paragraphs.text: A walk's average size grows with its length according to an exponent equal to one over its fractal dimension. That fractal dimension is 4/3 in two dimensions, close to 5/3 in three, and 2 once there are four or more dimensions. Likewise, the radius of gyration grows with length raised to the 3/4 power in two dimensions, and to roughly the 3/5 power in three. Above a certain dimension, called the upper critical dimension, excluded volume hardly matters, and in higher dimensions a SAW is thought to act much like an ordinary random walk.

paragraphs.heading: Trapped like the game Snake
paragraphs.text: In a growing self-avoiding walk, the walker starts at the origin of a lattice and keeps stepping, in a random direction, to an empty neighbouring site. If no neighbouring site is empty, the walk is trapped, much like the end of the video game Snake. Simulations show that on a square lattice this happens after about 71 steps on average. The figure is similar on a honeycomb lattice, near 78 on a triangular one, and close to 4000 on a simple cubic lattice in three dimensions.

paragraphs.heading: Knots in long loops
paragraphs.text: In three dimensions, self-avoiding polygons can be knotted. On a simple cubic lattice the shortest knotted one is a trefoil knot that uses 24 vertices. It has been proved that as these polygons get longer, the chance that one is not knotted falls off exponentially, so a long enough loop is almost certain to be knotted. On a face-centred cubic lattice, the odds of a knot reach one half at a length of roughly 100,000.
